newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: IRELAND'S RAPID GROWTH CONTINUES - ESRI.
newsitem.headline: IRELAND'S RAPID GROWTH CONTINUES - ESRI.

text.p: The economic outlook for Ireland should be reasonably favourable in both 1997 and 1998, the Economic and Social Research Institute (ESRI) said in a quarterly commentary published on Wednesday.
The ESRI, a state-funded research body, said that real GNP growth should rise by about 7.0 percent in 1997, compared with the annual average rise of 7.5 percent in the last three years.
It forecast a rise of just over 50,000 in employment and expected a further substantial improvement in the state's public finances.
The ESRI expected the government's Exchequer Borrowing Requirement (EBR) to fall to about 100 million Irish pounds or 0.2 percent of GNP.
The ESRI said it expected some slight acceleration in the rate of consumer price inflation in the second half of the year, leading to an annual average increase of about 1.75 percent.

"However, the achievement of the authorities in maintaining the Irish pound as one of the most stable currencies in Europe, on a trade-weighted basis, over the past 12 months should preclude a more rapid rise in prices in 1997," the ESRI said.
It warned that because of continuing currency instability in Europe, some uncertainty must surround economic forecasts for 1998.
"It is clear that the weakness of the mark and undue strength of sterling must ultimately be reversed, but the timing of this adjustment cannot be predicted with confidence," the ESRI said.

On the assumption that much of the adjustment would take place in 1998, and that the international strengthening of the mark might precede the weakening of sterling, "... it seems quite likely that the annual average trade-weighted value of the Irish pound could be moderately lower in 1998 than in 1997".

The ESRI said if this assumption is correct, then consumer price inflation in 1998 could rise to an annual average of about 2.5 percent and there could be a significant deterioration in the terms of trade and in the current account balance of payments surplus.

It said, however, the underlying strength of the economy was such that real GNP should continue to increase rapidly at a projected 6.75 percent, employment should rise by almost 40,000, and the EBR should be eliminated.
